## Work log

<!-- Chronological, written as you go. What was actually done, why, what it cost.
     Reference commits and link to plans and notes. Prose beats a checklist here —
     this is the part you will actually reread in three months. -->

- "We need the bridges in the printable model… they should just protrude and not have
  empty space below." The second clause is the design; the first is the easy part.
  `bridges.ts` builds a deck on piers with a void underneath, which is correct on screen
  and wrong on a plate: a span 2.5 mm up with air beneath it is an overhang, the slicer
  puts supports under every bridge, and the deck snaps when they come off. So the print
  reads `deckStations`' `top` and ignores its `bottom`. The underside of a printed bridge
  is the plate. It is a causeway rather than a bridge, and at 1:7,143 that is the honest
  trade.

- The ramps are what made this more than a filter. A flat top per segment steps down to
  the bank, and a step is both uglier and a worse overhang than the void being avoided —
  so `solid()` now takes a height FIELD as well as a height. Linear over the footprint,
  so the top face stays planar, the fan over the cap stays honest, and the cap-boundary
  walls still close. A corner cut off by a tile seam gets the height the ramp actually has
  at that point rather than its station's.

- Two things the screen version does that a plate cannot tolerate, both now guarded:
  `deckStations` buries its ramp ends at −0.6 m to hide a cut edge under the ground, which
  on a plate is a solid dangling below the bed (every vertex is clamped to the plate floor,
  with a test); and the ramp now ends at road level rather than at the plate, so a bridge
  and the street it carries are one solid.

- Decided that `roadMinWidthM` should NOT apply to bridges. It is a triangle budget for the
  scene's 36,460 road segments, and there are 48 bridges. Seven of the twelve inside the
  default crop are 2 m footpaths over the canals — most of how the riverbank is actually
  crossed. `MIN_BRIDGE_MM` widens any deck under 1 mm instead, so a 2 m footpath prints as
  7 m of model. That is a visible distortion, so it is stated in the download's README
  beside the height exaggeration.

- Costs 472 triangles across the four default tiles — 154,788 against 154,316. Bridges run
  1.80 to 4.53 mm: embedded 0.2 mm in the plate, 2.5 mm proud of it, against a 2.13 mm
  median building. Every bridge solid is watertight, seam-cut ones included, and the plan
  preview draws each deck so a crossing can be checked before a four-hour print.

- Afternoon turned into the backdrop. The question was "when does the switchover happen"
  and the answer is that there isn't one: the near/far split is spatial and baked into the
  committed document by the generator — 1,250 m of geometry, everything else raster — so
  zooming never swaps anything, it just magnifies. One texel is 4.80 m, and on a retina
  laptop that is ~1.25 device pixels at district fit, which is why it looks fine at the
  default view and soft immediately after.

- Worked out what a tile pyramid would actually buy, because it was worth knowing before
  agreeing to it. The structural point: **flat-sheet VRAM is set by how big the world is,
  a pyramid's by how big the screen is.** Zoom in 2× and the visible ground area quarters
  while the texel halves, so the texel count is constant. Pyramid plateaus at ~64 MB on a
  laptop and ~41 MB on a phone at any zoom; the flat sheet needs 120 MB at 2× fit, 480 MB
  at 4× and 1.9 GB at 8×. So a bigger sheet can never win — `--width 4096` buys one
  doubling and then the same wall. On the roadmap with the table, because re-deriving it
  would be a waste of an afternoon.

- Did NOT build it. It is a schema change plus a rewrite of `BackdropPlane.tsx`, and the
  doors open tomorrow. `docs/roadmap.md` already says the renderer gets rewritten before
  December and that the schema is one of the three things that must survive — this is
  precisely that kind of change.

- Shipped the escape hatch instead: **`?lod=full`** renders all 68,704 buildings as
  geometry and drops the raster. The raster exists because of the phone, and the laptop
  and projector are not the phone. One array swap — the viewer document already carries
  every road, water and green area, only buildings were ever stripped — plus a dynamic
  `import()` so the 19 MB document never touches a default load. Verified: a plain `/`
  fetches 3.2 MB and nothing else; `?lod=full` fetches the big one once; toggling back
  with `f` re-fetches nothing.

- **The measurement that changed how it is documented.** `mergeBuildings` is synchronous,
  so the switch freezes the main thread for 6.3 s (68,704 buildings → 998,168 triangles,
  72 MB of vertex buffers; the near set is 1.0 s and 112k). A full `?lod=full` load in dev
  took 26 s end to end. That is fine for a setting applied once when the installation
  starts and NOT fine as something to press during a show, so CLAUDE.md and the README
  both say start-of-day setting rather than live control. `f` exists for judging it on the
  machine, not in front of an audience.

- Left `merge.ts` alone on purpose. The obvious wins are chunking the merge across frames,
  dropping `computeVertexNormals`, and storing vertex colours as `Uint8` instead of
  `Float32` — which alone would halve 72 MB. All three are on the path the phone build
  uses, and tonight is the wrong night.

- Last thing: **`/settings`**. The ask was to have the detail setting somewhere other than
  a URL, and it is right — a parameter has to be retyped after any navigation, it is
  invisible once set, and "what is this machine configured to do?" has no answer except
  reading the address bar. `localStorage`, which with no server is the only option and also
  the correct granularity: settings belong to a MACHINE, and the laptop, the projector and
  a visitor's phone are three machines that want three different answers.

- Precedence is URL parameter > stored setting > default, and kept the parameters rather
  than replacing them: `?view=` is how a QR code aims at a view, which is older than this
  and still wanted. **The test worth having is that an ABSENT parameter does not clobber a
  stored setting** — the naive version, where every parameter falls back to a default,
  means that merely opening `/` wipes the machine's configuration, which would make
  settings strictly worse than the thing they replace.

- `f` had to start saving. A toggle that forgets is worse than no toggle: the machine looks
  configured and comes back wrong after a restart. It writes the whole settings object back
  so it cannot drop the other three fields.

- Verified against the **static export**, not the dev server, and that mattered. Default
  load 4.89 MB; configured for full geometry, 13.8 MB and `load` at 5.1 s, then the ~6 s
  merge. This morning's 26 s figure was Turbopack serving 19 MB of unminified JSON and was
  never what the laptop would do — corrected in that plan.

- Also spent twenty minutes chasing a ghost: the settings appeared not to apply at all, and
  the reason was a stale chunk from before the wiring compiled. A hard reload fixed it and
  nothing was wrong with the code. Worth remembering before debugging anything in dev: check
  the bundle actually contains what was just written.

- Deleted `hasViewParam` after writing, exporting and testing it. A stored view and a
  parameter view turn out to mean the same thing to the on-ramp, so it had no caller — an
  abstraction waiting for a use, which CLAUDE.md says to resist.

- **Afternoon: the exhibition artwork arrived and the spine changed shape.** Two separate
  things landed together. The printed panels (`CosmoLocal Exhibition_5.pdf`, 56 of them,
  141 MB — compressed to 14 MB beside it, and the text extracted) turn out to be the
  authority the screen answers to, not the brand concept deck `design-system.md` was
  derived from on the 16th. And a long conversation about scrollytelling ended somewhere
  quite different from where it started.

- **I was wrong about the palette, twice, in opposite directions.** First I sampled the KV
  marketing assets and concluded the brand had moved to cream and gold and away from
  orange. Then I extracted the *panels'* own span colours and fill operators rather than
  sampling pixels, and every value they use was already in `theme.ts` exactly —
  `#FF8A00`, `#2B184C`, `#1F1F1F`, `#FCFAF6`, IBM Plex Sans Thai. The apparent gold rail
  on p22 is Cosmo Orange with JPEG rounding. The cream is real but belongs to the pull-up
  banners, which are a different artefact. **Sampling a JPEG is not reading a design
  system.**

- What was actually wrong was the *register*. The panels put charcoal ink on near-white and
  reserve purple for one inverted panel; the app put purple text on off-white and had no
  kicker, no inverted panel and no rail. So `REGISTERS` — `page` and `invert` — composed
  entirely from Layer 1, adding roles without adding colours. `UI_TOKENS` are now the
  `page` register under their old names, which moves `ui.text` to charcoal.

- **`/design` earned its keep within an hour of existing.** It renders the system from
  `theme.ts`, so it cannot drift — and it immediately disproved the plan that had just been
  written. The plan assumed the print's kicker orange would clear 3:1 as large text and
  fail only at body size. Measured: **2.27:1 on the page ground, failing at every size.**
  The panels get away with it at 80 pt on paper under gallery light. A screen does not.
  Raw orange *does* pass on purple at 6.64:1, so `invert` keeps the wall colour and `page`
  derives one. The generalisable bit: **print contrast is not evidence about screen
  contrast**, and a page that renders the tokens is how you find that out in minutes rather
  than at the framing shop.

- **Chapters: past, present, futures — and a view owns a tense.** The scrollytelling
  conversation started as "three layers as scrolly chapters" and I spent the first answer
  defending a strawman nobody had raised (that this meant one continuous zoom) and
  overestimating the work by about three plans. Corrected on both. What it settled into:
  three scroll sequences, one per view, scroll scoped so it never crosses views, and the
  switcher unchanged. `views.ts` does not move.

- Then the real decision, and it is bigger than the chapters: **space is locked to time
  period.** Valley is the past, circle the present, city 2045 and only 2045. That kills the
  on-ramp, the idle reset to 2026, and "registers" as a concept — all three existed to
  describe a 2026 Wat Ket that no longer exists anywhere in the piece. The checkable form
  is that every view is a timeless substrate plus a period-bearing overlay: geology and
  building outlines have no tense, the claim is in the overlay, and GHS-POP *is* present
  data the way the DEM *is* timeless data.

- **Remote work is the seam, and it is structural rather than convenient.** River, roads and
  rail have alignments you could survey and they terminate in the basin. Remote work arrives
  from everywhere at once and its alignment is the internet, which is not geography. So the
  valley draws everything it is capable of drawing, and the one thread it cannot draw is the
  one that hands over to the circle. The exhibition panel already illustrates this without
  saying it — the plane enters on a dashed arc from off-frame while the river, road and rail
  are woven into the network.

- Written up as `plans/TODO.md` (twelve candidate plans), the design-system plan, and a
  research brief for the past chapter pinned to the valley's actual frame — origin
  18.7912N 99.0043E, ±60 km. The brief quotes the panels' own claims back for checking
  rather than restating them, and asks a fifth question outside the four threads: **is the
  three-storey conservation height limit real and still in force?** If it is, it constrains
  every 2045 scenario, which makes it the only finding that reaches forward out of the past.

- Carrying forward: **the `ui.text` change is not visually verified.** Charcoal instead of
  purple repainted every piece of chrome in the viewer and I only ever looked at `/design` —
  Chrome's screenshot tool would not inject into `/` (five attempts, three tabs; the diorama
  pegs the main thread past the 5 s window). Contrast is neutral-to-better numerically,
  15.06 → 15.81 on the page ground, but nobody has looked at it. Also: `.git/index.lock` was
  left behind twice by Cursor's git worker, zero bytes with no git process running.

## Notes

<!-- Decisions made, things learned, blockers, what carries into tomorrow.
     Anything that changes the project's direction belongs in CLAUDE.md or the architecture
     docs as well — the diary is the trail, not the source of truth. -->

- **A screen generator is not a print generator, even when the geometry is the same.**
  `bridges.ts` is reused for what it knows — which ways cross water, how wide a deck is,
  how high it sits by class — and overruled on what it assumes, which is that there is air
  under a bridge. Worth remembering the next time something is "just reused" for the plate:
  the parapets and piers are the next things that would need this treatment, and they are
  not in the print at all.

- **Settings are per machine, and that is a feature.** With no server there is nowhere else
  to put them, but per-machine is what an installation actually wants: three surfaces, three
  configurations, and a visitor's phone that has never heard of any of it.

- Carrying forward: print a tile. And **check `?lod=full` on the actual projector laptop
  before the doors open** — the 6 s switch is measured, but whether a million triangles
  holds a smooth frame rate afterwards is a property of that machine, not this one.

- **Flat-sheet VRAM scales with the world, a pyramid's with the screen.** That one sentence
  is why the backdrop cannot be fixed by making it bigger, and it is now on the roadmap
  with the table behind it.

- **The perf budget binds one surface, not three.** The raster, the viewer document and the
  1,250 m split all exist for the phone. Until today every surface paid the phone's price.
  `?lod=full` is the first place that stops being true, and it is worth remembering as a
  pattern: the budget in `docs/architecture.md` is a phone budget, and a laptop that is
  handed it for free is being short-changed.
